newsitem.title: GERMANY: Yugoslav opposition leader is German media darling.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav opposition leader is German media darling.

text.p: Zoran Djindjic, one of the leaders of the Serbian opposition coalition holding mass protests in Belgrade, was little known outside his country a few months ago but has quickly turned into Germany's newest media darling.

As the Zajedno (Together) coalition continues to attract tens of thousands of people to march peacefully through the streets of the Serbian capital, Djindjic is doing his utmost in Germany to be seen as the heir to Serbia's throne.

He speaks fluent German, learnt during several years at university in Frankfurt and Konstanz, and comes across as a modern Western-oriented politician in stark contrast to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, who is rarely seen or heard.
He even knows how to speak in media-friendly soundbites. "We will achieve reforms in our country, we will change the political scene," he declares.

But the well-groomed Djindjic has not always sounded as much like a Western democrat. He too has played the nationalist card in Serbian politics and his newspaper profilers have pressed him on his relations with Bosnian Serb leaders.
Articles point out Djindjic's good contacts with the Serb leadership in Pale, including Radovan Karadzic who has been indicted for war crimes, during the war.
Djindjic was seen at a rally of Karadzic's Serb Democratic Party in Banja Luka during the election campaign this summer.
But he stresses now he is a democrat and says of his Democratic Party, one of three that make up the Zajedno coalition: "We have no contacts with the Serbs in Bosnia".
But whether Djindjic would be prepared to ensure Karadzic was delivered to the International Tribunal in The Hague is another question.

"If those who gave the orders (for war crimes) are to be tried, then Milosevic and Croatian President Franjo Tudjman must go to court. They are the main culprits," Djindjic told the newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
"The charge sheet against Karadzic contains hardly anything concrete...The criteria he has been charged on must be clarified."

In a throwback to 1989 and 1990 when dissidents and opposition leaders from East Germany, Slovenia, Czechoslovakia and Croatia talked of their struggles on German television, Djindjic's face graces screens on a nightly basis and he has been the focus of many newspaper profiles.
But diplomats caution against comparing the intricacies of Balkan politics with what happened in Eastern Europe when popular discontent forced out communist governments.
They have said there are no clear successors to take over from Milosevic or Tudjman -- a situation Djindjic is evidently trying to change.
Milosevic is counting on the protests withering due to cold and boredom and there is little prospect of him yielding.

The United States, which has viewed Milosevic as central to its peacemaking efforts in Bosnia, was slow to express public support for the protesters and criticism of Milosevic's moves to rein them in. But this has changed in recent days.
When authorities closed down an independent radio station on Tuesday, the West took notice.
The United States and European states condemned the move and Washington said the "outer wall" of sanctions against Belgrade would remain until Serbia shows respect for democracy.
As Djindjic says: "America will not be patient for ever if (Milosevic) suppresses democracy in Serbia."
